en: The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Silent Illumination and Divine Transformation, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms within ten koṭis of buddha-fields. Their names were:
the youth Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva, and Caitya...
Bodhisattva Thunderous Sound, Bodhisattva Red Lotus Hand, Bodhisattva Sunlight, Bodhisattva Moonlight,
Bodhisattva Far-Dust Valiant, Bodhisattva Severer of All Evil Destinies, Bodhisattva Wisdom-Supreme-Wisdom, Bodhisattva Jewel-Supreme-Wisdom,
Bodhisattva Sentient-Being-Supreme-Wisdom, and Bodhisattva Fragrant Flower-Supreme-Wisdom.
Sākyamuni, the Bodhisattva Sun-Surpassing Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Moon-Surpassing Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Stainless-Surpassing Wisdom,
the Bodhisattva Vajra-Surpassing Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Far-Removed-from-Dust-Surpassing Wisdom,
the Bodhisattva All-Illuminating-Surpassing Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Bright Banner, the Bodhisattva High Banner, the Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, and the Bodhisattva Unattached Banner.
The Bodhisattvas: Gandhapuṣpadhvaja, Vimaladhvaja, Sūryadhvaja, Candradhvaja, Vigatarajodhvaja, Samantāloka-dhvaja, Tejorāśi, Ratnatejas, Mahāprajñātejas, and Jñānavajratejas.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Vimalatejaprabha, the Bodhisattva Sūryatejaprabha, the Bodhisattva Candratejaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Puṇyaparvatatejaprabha, the Bodhisattva Jñānāvabhāsatejaprabha, the Bodhisattva Samajayatejaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Garbhadhara, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, and the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha.
Sāgaramati, Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Candragarbha Bodhisattva,
Guṇaviśuddhigarbha Bodhisattva, Dharmamudrāgarbha Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsagarbha Bodhisattva, Samantagandhagarbha Bodhisattva,
Padmottaragarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryanetra Bodhisattva, and Viśuddhanetra Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Stainless Eye, the Bodhisattva Unattached Eye, the Bodhisattva Universally Seeing Eye, the Bodhisattva Beneficially Sharpened Eye,
the Bodhisattva Vajra Eye, the Bodhisattva Jewel Eye, the Bodhisattva Space Eye, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye,
the Bodhisattva Celestial Crown, and the Bodhisattva Dharma-realm Radiance Maṇi-jewel Crown.
Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva Wondrous Enlightenment Crown, Bodhisattva Universal Illumination Crown,
Bodhisattva Source of the Treasury of All Buddhas Crown, Bodhisattva Manifestation in All Worlds Crown,
Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Crown, Bodhisattva Invincible Crown, and Bodhisattva Equally Covering the Lion Thrones of All Tathāgatas Crown.
...the Bodhisattva Samantadharmadhātu-gaganaprabhāsa-ābhā-mukuṭa, the Bodhisattva Brahmendra-cūḍa,
the Bodhisattva Nāgendra-cūḍa, the Bodhisattva Sarvabuddha-nirmāṇaprabhāsa-cūḍa,
the Bodhisattva Suvibuddha-cūḍa, and the Bodhisattva Sarvapraṇidhānasāgara-svaranirghoṣa-maṇirājendra-cūḍa.
The Bodhisattva Sarvatryadhvasamatā-svaraghoṣa-śikhara-cūḍa, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha, the Bodhisattva Dūraraṇaprabha, the Bodhisattva Jyotirprabha,
and those whose heads were covered by mani-jewel nets and mani-banner kings consisting of the light and shadows of the miraculous transformations of all Tathāgatas;
Cūḍāmaṇi Bodhisattva; Sarvatathāgatadharmacakrasvaranirghoṣacūḍāmaṇi Bodhisattva; Sarvatathāgatamahāraśmimaṇḍalamahāmaṇiratnagarjitacūḍāmaṇi Bodhisattva;
Sarvagaganatalavyūhāvabhāsamaṇiratnavicitracūḍāmaṇi Bodhisattva; Dharmaprabha Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Pure Light, Bodhisattva Sun-Moon Light, Bodhisattva Miraculous Transformation Light,
Bodhisattva Celestial Light, Bodhisattva High Banner of Merit, Bodhisattva High Banner of Wisdom, Bodhisattva High Banner of Supernatural Powers,
Bodhisattva High Banner of Radiance, Bodhisattva High Banner of Fragrant Flowers, and Bodhisattva High Banner of Maṇi.
Dhvaja Bodhisattva, Jñānottaradhvaja Bodhisattva, Brahmottaradhvaja Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsottaradhvaja Bodhisattva,
Brahmaghoṣa Bodhisattva, Nādadhara-ghoṣa Bodhisattva, Sāgaraghoṣa Bodhisattva, Lokendraghoṣa Bodhisattva,
Sarvamahāparvatarājasaṃghaṭṭanaghoṣa Bodhisattva, and Sarvadharma... [Bodhisattvas].
The Bodhisattva Sound Pervading All Realms, the Bodhisattva Sound of the Thunder of the Ocean of All Dharmas,
the Bodhisattva Subduer of All Māra-Wheels, the Bodhisattva Sound of the Cloud-Thunder of the Principle of Great Compassion,
the Bodhisattva Sound Consoling the Suffering of All Sentient Beings, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Samudgata, the Bodhisattva Jina-Samudgata, and the Bodhisattva Jñāna-Samudgata.
The Bodhisattva Puṇyasumerūdgata, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati-udgata, the Bodhisattva Yaśas-udgata,
the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhā-udgata, the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitry-udgata, the Bodhisattva Jñānābhāsa-udgata,
the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotra-udgata, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-jaya, the Bodhisattva Sūkṣma-jaya, and the Bodhisattva Janma-jaya.
Samantāloka-vijaya Bodhisattva, Gaganavijaya Bodhisattva, Ratnavijaya Bodhisattva,
Uccadhvaja-vijaya Bodhisattva, Jñānavijaya Bodhisattva, Uccapati-rāja Bodhisattva,
Lokapati-rāja Bodhisattva, Brahmapati-rāja Bodhisattva, Parvatapati-rāja Bodhisattva, and Acalapati-rāja Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Honored Lord King, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Enlightenment Lord King, the Bodhisattva Tranquil Sound, the Bodhisattva Unattached Sound,
the Bodhisattva Sustaining Sound, the Bodhisattva Ocean Tide Sound, the Bodhisattva Original Vow Enlightenment Sound,
the Bodhisattva Path-Place Sound, the Bodhisattva High Wisdom Enlightenment, and the Bodhisattva Space Enlightenment.
The Bodhisattvas— Vimalabodhi, Asaṅgabodhi, Vibodhabodhi, Tryadhvāvabhāsabodhi, Ratnabodhi, Vipulabodhi, Samantaprabhabodhi, and Dharmadhātunayāvabhāsabodhi— such as these were the leaders.

At the head [of the assembly] were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten koṭis of Buddha-fields, all of whom dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression. They had all fully accomplished the immeasurability of the realm of space and accomplished the unobstructed equality of the Dharma-realm. They possessed the conviction that the maturation arising from karma is according to its conditions, and the conviction that all fruits arising from causes are like seals being impressed—whereby all phenomena are produced;

they possessed the Wisdom of Equality which perceives all phenomena as being like light, shadows, and reflections, and through the nature of equality, they perceived all phenomena as identical to the resonance of an echo, thereby manifesting the nature of equality.

They have all attained the supreme meditative concentration of inconceivable liberation and abide in the *cāritra* samādhis; they abide in the ability to manifest the forms and images of infinite Buddha-bodies.
They have perfected all dhāraṇīs and are able to universally manifest all buddha-fields within a single pore, and to universally manifest within a single pore either passing away or being born:

emerging from the womb, leaving home, skillfully demonstrating the practice of difficult and painful austerities, proceeding to the seat of enlightenment to subdue the demonic armies, attaining equal and perfect awakening, turning the wheel of the true Dharma, and finally manifesting entry into great parinirvāṇa.

Having achieved the single seated cross-legged posture, they possess the wisdom that can universally pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions; they manifest as a single Tathāgata within all the assemblies of all Tathāgatas in all worlds throughout the ten directions, and within the assembly of a single Tathāgata, they can universally manifest all Tathāgatas;
they are skillful in expounding upon the boundless middle of all phenomena, and have reached the infinite limits of all phenomena.
Entering into various nets of illusion within the infinite, he is able to universally manifest sentient beings throughout boundless and limitless eons;
he possesses skillful mastery in the resolute conviction that can universally penetrate and sustain the bodies of all sentient beings within his own body;
and he possesses skillful mastery in the resolute conviction that can universally penetrate and sustain the bodies of all Tathāgatas within a single body.
They are able to universally penetrate and enter into a single Buddha-body, manifesting the bodies of all Tathāgatas, and are skillful in all other sentient beings' bodies without exception.
They are able to universally penetrate their own bodies, skillfully manifesting all worlds throughout the ten directions;

they are able to universally manifest within a single dharma-body, pervading all sentient beings of the three periods of time; they are able to enter samādhi with a single body and manifest the emergence of the bodies of infinite sentient beings;

they realize equal enlightenment within a single body and can universally manifest bodies identical to those of all sentient beings; within the bodies of all those sentient beings, they can universally manifest the body of a single sentient being, and furthermore, within the body of a single sentient being, they can universally manifest the bodies of all sentient beings.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, they can manifest the Dharma-body; within the Dharma-body, they can manifest the bodies of sentient beings.

They are able, among all the vows of Bodhisattvas, to awaken to and abide in the skillful means of the vowless; they can manifest for sentient beings the manifest realization of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) of all Buddhas, and the manifest realization of equal enlightenment within the sphere of the power of their vows.

For those classes of sentient beings who have already been matured, according to what is appropriate for their transformation, they can manifest unexcelled perfect enlightenment and can bring to rest all calculations of kalpas regarding the vowless.
Within the bodies of all sentient beings, they are able to universally manifest the sovereign power of their vows, transferring the consciousness-body and establishing the wisdom-body;
they are able to universally manifest the cessation of their own bodies while fulfilling the aspirations of the bodies of other sentient beings;
and they are able to universally manifest the accomplishment of the great vows of all sentient beings.
Within each and every world, they are able to manifest all kalpas, practicing the bodhisattva path without interruption;
through the power of great vows, they can manifest throughout all buddha-lands from a single pore;
and within each and every one of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds, they are universally able to manifest their bodies and attain equal, perfect enlightenment.
Within a single phrase of the Dharma, they are able to universally manifest and proclaim it without exception, pervading the entire realm of phenomena;
they can rain down the vast flow of the Dharma, producing the wondrous taste of ambrosia;
they can universally illuminate all clarities and liberations, thundering with the true sound of the Dharma’s thunderclap to satisfy the realms of all sentient beings and fulfill their great vows.
They are universally able to awaken to and enter the spheres of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the domain of wise insight;

with the mere arising of a single thought, they can manifest the various distinctions of the physical forms of all sentient beings born within the places of birth, death, and transmigration throughout all worlds in the ten directions;

and they have attained mastery in the unhindered knowledge of their own minds, the knowledge of others' minds, the mind of a single sentient being, and the wisdom that knows the movements of the minds of all sentient beings.
In a single kṣaṇa, they attain mastery in skillfully realizing the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata’s ten powers;

they universally attain mastery in skillfully realizing the unimpeded wisdom that penetrates all kalpas throughout the three periods of time, as well as the sublime wisdom that manifests the mental continuums of other sentient beings;
and in each and every moment of mind, they attain mastery in skillfully manifesting all sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions wherever they may dwell.
Furthermore, they attain mastery in the sublime wisdom that directly perceives all the karmic activities of all sentient beings by means of a single thought-moment regarding one sentient being;
they attain mastery in the sublime wisdom that penetrates and manifests the speech and sounds of all sentient beings by means of the speech and sounds produced by one sentient being;
and they attain mastery in universally manifesting all bodies existing in all worlds by taking a single body as their basis.
Within the assembly of a single Tathāgata, they attain skillfulness in realizing and manifesting the assemblies of all Tathāgatas, as well as their preaching of the Dharma and its upholding;

they attain skillfulness in realizing and manifesting within the assemblies of all Tathāgatas the preaching of the Dharma and its upholding within the assembly of a single Tathāgata; they attain all sublime dhāraṇīs and realize the eloquence of firm determination that sustains them, attaining skillfulness in proclaiming the faculties of the entire realm of sentient beings;

taking the mind of a single sentient being as their object of focus, they undergo an ineffable transformation to realize great Bodhi, attaining skillfulness in awakening to the mental wisdom of all sentient beings.

They possess mastery in being able to universally instruct all worlds with a single vocal sound; they possess mastery in being able to fully comprehend the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings and in illuminating the mental continuums of other beings;

they possess mastery in being able to enter, through a single moment of mindfulness, into the number of kalpas from the past of all sentient beings, universally manifesting the maturation of the fruits of the karma they have performed, and awakening sentient beings according to their needs so that they may all clearly perceive it;
and they possess mastery in being able to universally adorn all worlds.

They have attained mastery in skillfully entering into all worlds; they have awakened to the equality of all Buddhas; they have attained mastery in universally knowing how to emit the light of the Dharma through the essential practice of the great vows of Bodhisattvas;
they have attained mastery in causing unspeakably many worlds to enter into a single minute atom;
and they have attained mastery in making the measure of a single minute atom equal to all worlds.
They have attained mastery in being able to universally manifest all Buddha-lands within a single Buddha-land;

they have attained mastery in placing the vast masses of water from all oceans inside a single pore and traveling back and forth through worlds as numerous as the measure of the Dharma-realm without harming or distressing any class of sentient beings;

and they have attained mastery in causing all that exists in unspeakable numbers of worlds to enter their own bodies, while universally manifesting all the activities performed by all sentient beings.

They possess mastery in being able to place within a single pore countless, inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable Lesser Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), Great Iron Ring Mountains, and other great mountains, traveling back and forth through all worlds without causing any fear among sentient beings;

they possess mastery in condensing unspeakably unspeakable eons into a single eon, and extending a single eon into unspeakably unspeakable eons, while universally manifesting therein the various distinctions of formation and destruction;

and for the sake of the sentient beings to be converted, they possess mastery in universally manifesting, as appropriate within all distinct worlds, either a calamity of water, a calamity of fire, or a calamity of wind.
They possess mastery in lifting and tossing countless, inconceivable, and immeasurable worlds with the tip of their right toe without causing harm or distress to any sentient beings;

they have all already attained the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) and possess mastery in sustaining all the vast calamities, afflictions, famines, and perils of the sentient beings to be converted throughout the ten directions, without harming other beings;
and by means of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), they are able to manifest the appearance of a Buddha in worlds where no Buddha currently resides.
Thus, he had fully accomplished these immeasurable and boundless merits.
Furthermore, he was accompanied by five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla as their leader; all of them resided in the stage of non-retrogression.

At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was a Licchavi youth named Ratnākara, who, surrounded by twenty-one thousand other Licchavi youths, went to Vulture Peak Mountain to the place where the Tathāgata was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to the right, and remained there with reverence, gazing up at the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for even a moment.

In the great city of Kajaṅghala, there was a householder named Śama, who, surrounded by five hundred upāsakas, proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain. Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and gazed upon the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for even a moment, remaining there with profound reverence.

Furthermore, there was a householder named Well-Tamed (Suvinita), who, surrounded by five thousand householders, went to Vulture Peak Mountain and approached the Tathāgata. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and gazed up at the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for even a moment, remaining there in reverent attendance.

Furthermore, there was a householder named Śreṣṭhin who, accompanied by a great retinue and surrounded by them from front and back, went to Vulture Peak Mountain. Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, he prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and gazed up at the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for a moment, remaining there with reverence.

In the great city of Campā, there was an elder’s son named Subāhu, who, surrounded by eighty-four thousand sons of elders, proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain. Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and gazed upon the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for a moment, remaining there with reverent devotion.

Furthermore, there was a young brahmin named Naradatta, who, surrounded by five hundred young brahmins, went to Vulture Peak Mountain to the place where the Tathāgata was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and gazed up at the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for a moment, remaining there with reverent devotion.

Furthermore, there was a māṇavaka named Ruci who, accompanied by five hundred other māṇavakas and surrounded by them from front and back, went to Vulture Peak Mountain. He approached the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and gazed upon the World-Honored One without blinking for a moment, remaining there with reverence.

The King of Magadha, named Ajātaśatru, surrounded by a retinue of five thousand, mounted the elephant king Dhanapāla and proceeded toward Vulture Peak Mountain. Having traveled as far as the ground would allow on the elephant Dhanapāla, he reached the palace pavilion, dismounted from the elephant with both feet, and ascended Vulture Peak Mountain. Together with his five thousand followers, he approached the Tathāgata, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. Gazing up at the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for even a moment, he remained there in reverent attendance.

In the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was the son of a householder named Śubhadeśa, who, together with five hundred sons of householders, surrounded him on all sides and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain. Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, gazed upon the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for even a moment, and remained there in reverent attendance.

Furthermore, there were Śakra, King of Devas; Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā World; the Four World-Protecting Kings; Maheśvara, Son of Heaven; Sūrya and Candra, Sons of Heaven; Sudhīramati, Son of Heaven; Susīmā, Son of Heaven; and countless other inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless sons of heaven. Each of these sons of heaven was accompanied by an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of celestial attendants, surrounding them from front and behind as they proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain to the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrating at his feet.

Each of the sons of heaven, having individually presented inconceivable and wondrous offerings according to their respective capacities, withdrew to sit at one side; they gazed up at the World-Honored One without averting their eyes for even a moment, remaining there in reverent attendance.

At that time, from each and every pore, each and every minor mark, and each and every major mark of the World-Honored One, there issued forth various colored rays of light, as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields.
Each of these individual rays of light universally illumines ten *koṭi* of worlds, as numerous as the atoms of dust in each of the ten directions, pervading them all without exception.
From each and every world, he summoned countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas.

Each of these Bodhisattvas was mounted upon a sublime jewel terrace, surrounded by jeweled pavilions extending for a hundred *koṭis* of *yojanas* in both length and breadth. These were exquisitely adorned with cords of *maṇi* and genuine jewels, and graced with high banners, flags, and canopies. Surrounded before and behind by immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* celestial maidens, they proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain to the presence of the Tathāgata. There they prostrated at his feet and, holding clouds of various heavenly flowers, clouds of jewels, clouds of robes, clouds of firm *candanana* incense as vast as worlds, and clouds of celestial music and songs of praise, they scattered them as offerings. Then, withdrawing to sit to one side, they gazed upon the World-Honored One without blinking for a moment, remaining there in reverent attendance.

At that time, in this trichiliocosm, gods of vast majesty and power, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, humans, non-humans, and the assembly of bodhisattvas stood packed together, so that there was not even a space the size of a hair-tip that was not filled.

At that time, from within the assembly, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I wish to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding a few matters.
I pray only that you grant me permission to answer what I have asked.
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, saying:
“Bhadrapāla! Ask whatever you desire; let your questions be as you wish.
I shall answer accordingly to bring joy to your heart.”
When these words had been spoken, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By virtue of what place, by practicing what conduct, by following what rules, by what roots of goodness, by what diligence, by what reliance, by what skillful wisdom, by what sublime knowledge, by what mindfulness, by what destination, by what inducement, by what upheld truth, and by what armor, do the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas become neither turning back nor retreating, nor experiencing total regression from their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but instead advance with courageous vigor toward that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?”
What is the Tathāgata’s practice of blazing diligence?
What is the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom?
And what is great intelligence and skill in wisdom?
What is pure ethical discipline?
What is the possession of mindfulness, such that one does not forget or lose the teachings as they are heard?
What is the arising of mindfulness, such that one can fully comprehend all the roots of goodness performed in previous lives?
How does one attain skillfulness regarding past lives and thereby fully awaken all other sentient beings?
How does one possess the excellence of awakened faculties?
How does one possess the marks [of a Buddha], see the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and serve the Saṅgha?

How does one, while dwelling in other worlds, universally behold the Buddhas of boundless and limitless worlds, hear their teachings and retain them all with ultimate mastery and proficiency, and extensively proclaim, explain, and reveal them for others?
How shall I attain that which is like a flame, capable of burning away all unwholesome roots?
How shall I attain that which is like the bright moon, capable of realizing all fresh, white, and pure dharmas?
How shall I come to be like the king of mountains, able to sustain all supreme roots of goodness?
How shall I come to be like a diamond, profoundly patient and indestructible?
How shall one attain fearlessness, like the peak of a mountain?
How shall one attain a perfectly pure voice and eloquence free from obstruction?
How shall one attain the fulfillment of extensive learning, with definitive skill in analyzing all phenomena?
How shall one obtain a face that is well-purified and always smiling, remaining free from frowning?
How shall one become free from envy and stinginess?
How shall one be able to proclaim teachings with one's voice throughout infinite worlds?

How can all that exists within infinite and boundless worlds be placed within a single pore, such that the sentient beings therein cannot perceive where they have gone, except for those who are ready to be delivered, who can correctly understand it?
How is it that within the great assemblies of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions, one can universally manifest the ripening of sentient beings without moving from one’s original location?

How is it that one can manifest—in a single pore—the passing away from the Tuṣita heaven, dwelling in the womb, birth, leaving the city for renunciation, practicing asceticism, proceeding to the seat of enlightenment, subduing the armies of Māra, attaining equal and perfect awakening, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma, and entering great parinirvāṇa, thereby manifesting the endurance of the True Dharma?
"How should one attain a single moment of mind that can fully comprehend all the mental activities of all sentient beings?
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Bhadrapāla! Excellent!
That you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning is truly commendable.

The practice you are now undertaking is for the sake of benefiting many sentient beings, for the sake of bringing happiness to many sentient beings, out of compassion for the great multitudes of the world, and to bring about great benefit and peace for all devas and humans.
"You have now accomplished great compassion.
Therefore, Bhadrapāla!
Listen attentively now and apply your mind with great care; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla said: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"

There is a samādhi called "Quiescent Illumination and Divine Transformation," which is practiced by bodhisattvas and subsumed within the stage of Buddhahood. When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells securely within this, they are able to attain these and other immeasurable, preeminent merits.
Bhadrapāla! What is called the samādhi of tranquil illumination and spiritual transformation?
It refers to being able to realize all phenomena as they truly are, penetrating their characteristics and penetrating the characteristic of non-inversion.
He penetrates the characteristics of perversion, augmenting the characteristics of non-perversion and diminishing the characteristics of perversion;
he does not cling to his own stage of abiding nor grasp at the stages of others’ abiding;
he does not rely upon life, and does not transmigrate within birth and death; he thoroughly knows all phenomena and practices *śamatha* until it becomes manifest.
As the practice of vipaśyanā meditation becomes manifest, the mind dwells in stability; mindfulness is free from distraction, and discursive thought and investigation are stilled.
One distances oneself from unwholesome factors and draws near to wholesome ones, ceasing greed, hatred, and delusion.
One eliminates ignorance and approaches clarity, thoroughly understanding cause and effect and distancing oneself from them.

Free from ignorance, he has forever exhausted craving and eternally severed delight and greed; he is certain regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and possesses deep faith in the Saṃgha.
His speech is non-divisive, he harmonizes with others, and his inclinations lead toward seclusion.
His words are exquisite and his countenance is upright; free from attachment to flavors, he commits no evil deeds and is supported by [virtuous] provisions.
They assist in the separation from and the distancing of fetters; they do not give rise to attachment or delight in worldly affairs;
they perceive the profound faults and perils of saṃsāra and the supreme virtues of nirvāṇa, and through their superior intention, they take pleasure in parinirvāṇa.

Free from flattery and crookedness, free from illusion and deception; without hypocrisy, without deceitful speech, without feigned appearances, and without fraudulent investigation; always delighting in avoiding wealth, profit, and honor; courageous, diligent, and supremely patient; without indolence and having forever severed all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); constantly rejoicing in encountering the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*); with the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) unimpaired and the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*) unshakable; entering into meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) without dependence; never being satiated in fulfilling the *pāramitās*; possessing mastery over the transformation of dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments; sporting at will through the various bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); and turning with mastery toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) with excellent discerning awakening.

By nature he is not dull-witted; by nature he is not mute; he is not under the command of others. Regarding long-standing affairs, his nature is able to remain detached. He dwells with virtuous persons and does not look toward evil persons; he stays far away from fools and delights in meeting the wise. He maintains the power of mindfulness and maintains the power of wisdom. He takes no pleasure in living at home or mingling with those who have left the household life, but delights in dwelling in seclusion. He is able to correctly endure the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and he penetrates all dharmas as they truly are.
Bhadrapāla! This is called the samādhi of the miraculous transformation of tranquil illumination.
When a bodhisattva diligently practices and trains in this samādhi, they attain unobstructed wisdom regarding all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
As for the samādhi of the miraculous transformation of tranquil illumination, it refers to the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena and the wisdom in which no verbal expressions manifest."
Having renounced domestic affairs and taking no pleasure in the three realms, they are free from weakness or despondency;
their minds have no attachment to any phenomena (*dharma*), and they embrace the True Dharma while secretly protecting all teachings.

They develop deep faith and understanding in the maturation (*vipāka*) of dharmas, possess skillful means regarding the Vinaya, and bring all disputes to rest, being without contradiction or contention, and patient.

The equality of sensation and the equality of the destination; skill in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), skill in the determination of phenomena, and skill in the phrases of the Dharma;

the wisdom that analyzes the phrases of the Dharma; the wisdom that knows the past limit, the wisdom that knows the future limit, the wisdom of the purity of the three spheres, the wisdom of the body’s stable abiding, the wisdom of the mind’s stable abiding, the wisdom of maintaining dignified deportment, and regarding the Dharma—
Purity surpasses the thorough knowledge of the aggregates as objects of perception; the wisdom of the equality of the elements illuminates all sense bases;
craving is forever severed as one proceeds toward the realization of non-arising; one clearly perceives the destruction of karma and its fruits within their causes;
seeing the Dharma and cultivating the path, one joyfully encounters the Tathāgata; with the nature of sharp wisdom, one discriminates the knowledge of syllables and thoroughly knows all sounds.
Having realized the Dharma, their joy and rapture never diminish. They are supple and upright, free from frowning;

they are gentle, harmonious, compliant, and pleasant, being the first to speak with words of welcome, remaining free from all indolence. They show reverence and respect, listening attentively to the teacher’s instructions.

They find no satisfaction in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), but are fully endowed with pure and bright qualities (*śukladharma*). Their lives are pure, and they do not abandon the state of tranquil abiding (*śamatha-vihāra*). They are established in the superior stages, with unimpaired right mindfulness. They possess skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*). They proceed toward the realization of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the diminution of all afflictions (*kleśa*), forever destroying the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). They advance toward higher progress, cultivating and accomplishing [the path].

He is skillful in means regarding the methods for emerging from the various transgressions; he is able to forever subdue the fetters of all views; he cuts off the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) without emerging [from the path]; he possesses the recollection of past lives; he has no doubt regarding the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*); he does not entrust his mind to any phenomena; he does not apply effort toward any worldly activities; he does not direct his attention toward the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), nor does he engage with the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*); he does not exalt himself nor disparage others; he has no attachment to any virtues; and he never entrusts himself to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Their ethical discipline (*śīla*) is a natural outflow that is difficult to achieve yet capable of being accomplished; they possess a great mass of light and are able to know themselves. Free from all agitation, they establish themselves in various dignified postures; they are without anger and remain free from harsh speech. They do not harm or vex others, but follow and protect virtuous friends. Remaining far removed from enmity and injury, they possess pure ethical discipline; they cause no harm and their speech is gentle. They do not rely on the three realms but guard their intimacy; they accord with and endure the emptiness and selflessness of all phenomena. Possessing a fierce and keen aspiration for the knowledge of all-knowledge, they illuminate with the light of wisdom this firm ethical discipline.

Entering into various meditative attainments, they always delight in dwelling alone; their non-conceptual wisdom is perfected in joy and contentment, and their minds are undisturbed and free from the activity of views.

Having attained the *dhāraṇīs* that lead into sublime wisdom, they possess correct understanding and practice regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*). Through the gateways of causal principles, they provide instruction and admonition; they are able to correctly practice in accordance with the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), remaining far removed from impatience and establishing themselves on the ground of wisdom. They forever sever ignorance and establish sublime wisdom—the conduct of Bodhisattvas on the stages of yoga. Reaching the sublime wisdom of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, they incinerate and wash away their minds so that nothing arises or continues.

Possessing unimpeded wisdom, they do not carry the heavy burden [of afflictions]. The sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata heals greed, removes hatred, and forever severs delusion; it harmonizes with correct principle and distances itself from what is irrational. Desiring wholesome dharmas, they practice superior intention and draw near to awakening. Without abandoning cessation, they guard the white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), possessing roots of goodness as their primary focus and skillful means.

Having permanently severed all signs and transformed all conceptualizations, they bring forth the sūtras and the excellent vinaya; through definitive discernment regarding the truths, they proceed toward the realization of liberation. Their speech is fixed and cannot be led astray by conditions; they give rise to such knowledge and vision as accord with reality, and they joyfully seek extensive learning with an insatiable wisdom.

“His mind is pure, his body is pure, and his speech is pure, free from doubt; he dwells in emptiness, draws near to signlessness, and has no grasping or attachment toward the nature of wishlessness. Having attained fearlessness, he does not disparage those who suffer in the realms of existence, and he bestows gifts of wealth and treasures upon them.”

He does not revile or reject those who are impoverished; toward those who have transgressed the precepts, he gives rise to a sense of compassion and undertakes actions for their benefit. He gathers them through the Dharma rather than by bestowing material wealth. Toward those who uphold the precepts, he offers praise without guile. He is able to relinquish all that he himself possesses, inviting others with a superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), and acts exactly as he has spoken.
Repeatedly initiating intense application and receiving [the teachings] with reverence and joy, one accomplishes the wisdom of analogies (*aupamya-jñāna*).

Skillfulness regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta-kauśalya*) is designated as a mere conventional designation (*prajñapti*); the wisdom capable of penetrating this permanently eliminates such designations. One does not hope for honor nor resent lack of honor; one seeks no gain and feels no grief at loss; one does not rejoice in praise, nor feel resentment when reviled; one does not crave fame, nor become dejected when disparaged; one does not indulge in pleasure, nor turn away from suffering; and one does not cling to any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding genuine praise, they do not become attached; regarding false praise, they do not grasp at it. They avoid what is improper to practice and engage in what is proper to practice; they draw near to true guides and distance themselves from those who are not guides. They never disparage or belittle sentient beings who possess even a small root of virtue, and they are able to correctly protect and uphold the Buddha’s holy teachings.
His speech was concise and his nature was gentle; he was skillful in the expedient means of worldly discourse, able to subdue adversaries and act with timely precision.
His deportment was pure and his bearing was dignified; he possessed the skillful wisdom that distinguishes between what is meaningful and what is not.

He thoroughly understands the world and is proficient in all treatises and modes of expression; he delights in practicing generosity and is ever ready to extend his hand, possessing a mind free from attachment and endowed with a sense of shame and moral dread.

He constantly feels revulsion for and disparages all unwholesome states of mind; he never abandons the virtues of *dhūta* (ascetic purification); he maintains right conduct and manifests straightforwardness; he rises to respectfully greet those worthy of honor; he offers seats and subdues pride; his mind is consistently exerted so as to penetrate their meaning; he embraces wisdom and brings rest to ignorance; he enters into the wisdom of the mind; regarding the nature of the mind itself, he possesses the wisdom of subsequent realization; he achieves skillful wisdom in what leads toward liberation, what does not, and in the process of inducing realization; he possesses the sublime wisdom of the speech of all sentient beings; he possesses the sublime wisdom that establishes various forms of expression; he possesses the wisdom that discerns meanings and remains far removed from what is meaningless; and while he distinguishes the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), he has no craving for their flavor.

He observes the minds of all sentient beings; he possesses the sublime wisdom that knows the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings; he is able to correctly observe what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); he is able to correctly discern all karmic actions; and he enters into sublime wisdom regarding that which is not karma and not maturation (*vipāka*).

He enters into and does not forget the various inclinations; he correctly perceives the various realms as well as the non-dual realm; in the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), there is nothing to be observed; and he possesses the Brahma-voice, meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*).

Regarding each and every instance of past lives, whether named or unnamed, there is the knowledge of recollecting them; there is the knowledge of correctly observing the pervasive formations; and there is the knowledge of attaining the realization of the permanent severance of the outflows.

With unimpeded divine vision, they universally and correctly observe, manifesting the playful mastery of supernatural powers in all forms, entering the wisdom of equality regarding both form and the formless.
They thoroughly comprehend the various components of speech and sounds, being able to accord with and enter the wisdom of *dhāraṇī* regarding all physical images, echoes, and vocal sounds.

The Wisdom of Equality proclaims the True Dharma as appropriate to each; it is the wisdom that skillfully teaches all sentient beings so they may rejoice, the wisdom of turning [the faculties], and the wisdom that contemplates the opportune and inopportune times to enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Whatever Dharma he teaches is never in vain; it is able to fulfill all the pāramitās and possesses the skillful wisdom that exerts effort and subdues all sentient beings.

"Regarding all modes of deportment, there is no conceptual differentiation; it is the sublime wisdom that flows within the undifferentiated realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), which destroys all conceptualization and manifold discrimination.
— *The Sutra on the Samādhi of Silent Illumination and Divine Transformation* (Jizhao shenbian sanmei jing)
